text: Before a model can answer a question about your documents, that data has to live somewhere — and for AI workloads on Azure, it usually lives in two different places doing two different jobs.

Raw documents land in Blob Storage first — PDFs, transcripts, images, whatever the source material actually is. A container is just a named bucket inside a storage account; cheap, durable, and completely unaware that any of this will eventually feed a model. This is where a lot of AI projects should start and usually don't — a well-organized place for the raw files before anyone talks about embeddings.

Getting a file in is as simple as uploading it through the portal, the CLI, or an SDK, with access tier and blob type set per upload. These are the same raw documents a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, covered back in Lesson 8, will later chunk into passages and turn into vectors.

The embeddings themselves don't live in Blob Storage at all — they're written into a search index, like Azure AI Search, with its own schema: a field for the original text, metadata fields to filter or sort on, and a vector field for the embedding, queried by similarity rather than keyword.
Two storage layers, two jobs — Blob Storage holds the raw material, a search index holds it chunked and embedded and ready to query.
Next up: making sure only the right things can actually reach either one.
